::: {.lead}
A player meets all the media of a game at the same time: a theme tune, a
flash of light, a line of dialogue, a health bar that turns red. A media
designer must learn to take this experience apart. In this lesson you learn a
method in three steps to analyse the media of any game: list the media, find
the job of each one, and decide if it is inside or outside the game world. You practise every step on a game that you
play yourself, and on *Ember Trail*, a made-up game about a young fox.
:::

## Key terms

{{< glossary media-channel art-style sound-effect ambience feedback diegetic player-experience >}}

## 2.1 The media inventory

The first step is to describe, not to judge. We make an **inventory**: a list
of all the media that the game uses, sorted by **media channel**. Five
channels cover almost every game (@fig-annotated):

- **visual**: the **art style** (the same shapes, colours and proportions
  everywhere), characters, places, animation, visual effects;
- **audio**: music, **sound effects** (SFX), voices and **ambience** (the
  background sound of a place, such as wind or rain);
- **text and story**: dialogue, item names, the story in words;
- **cinematic**: cut-scenes, intro videos and trailers, where the player
  watches instead of playing;
- **interface**: menus, buttons, icons and the HUD (head-up display) that
  shows health, score or time.

![An annotated screen of the mobile game Ember Trail. Each number marks one media element of the inventory.](images/annotated-screen.png){#fig-annotated width=94%}

An inventory is easiest as a table: one row for each element, with its
channel, a short description and the moment when it appears.

::: {.callout-note title="Example 2.1 — Inventory of one screen"}
The screen of *Ember Trail* in @fig-annotated contains:

1. a fox drawn in a soft, round art style (visual);
2. a campfire with moving flames and a crackling sound (visual, audio);
3. a health bar and a coin counter at the top (interface);
4. a speech bubble: "The bridge is out!" (text and story);
5. a floating "+10" above a collected coin (interface, visual effect);
6. flute music and the sound of wind (audio).

The inventory is complete when every element that reaches the player's eyes
or ears has a row.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Inventory of your game"}
Choose a game on your phone. Take a screenshot of one busy moment.

1. Make a table with three columns: element, channel, when it appears.
2. Write at least six rows. Use all five channels if you can.

*Your result:* the screenshot and the table. Keep both: you need them in the
next tasks.
:::

## 2.2 The functions of media

In a good game, every media element has a job. Five jobs, or **functions**,
appear again and again (@tbl-functions).

| Function | The player's question | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **feedback** | What happened because of my action? | a chime and a flash when I collect a coin |
| **guidance** | Where should I go? What can I use? | a glowing door, a lit path |
| **mood** | How should this moment feel? | slow music in a sad scene, rain sounds |
| **story** | What is happening? Who are these people? | dialogue, a cut-scene, a broken statue |
| **identity** | Which game is this? | a theme tune, a logo, a clear art style |

: The functions of media in games. {#tbl-functions}

One element often has several functions. A short trumpet tune at the end of a
level is feedback (the level is complete), mood (victory) and identity
(players know the game by it).

![One coin, three functions: the sound sets the mood, the "+10" gives feedback, and the next coins guide the player.](images/media-functions.png){#fig-functions width=94%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 2.2 — The functions of the “+10”"}
In *Ember Trail*, a collected coin shows a floating "+10", plays a bright
"ting" and adds to the counter (@fig-functions).

1. **Feedback**: the player sees at once that the action worked, and how much
   it was worth.
2. **Guidance**: coins lie along the safe path, so the next shining coin
   shows where to jump.
3. **Mood**: the bright, rising sound feels like a reward.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Describing instead of analysing. "There is music in the menu" only describes.
"The slow flute music in the menu makes the player calm before play begins"
analyses: it names the element, its function and its effect on the player.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · The jobs of your media"}
Use the inventory of your game.

1. Choose three elements from your table.
2. For each one, write its function (or functions) and one sentence about its
   effect on the player.

*Your result:* three analytic sentences, like the good sentence in the
common mistake above.
:::

## 2.3 Inside or outside the game world: diegetic and non-diegetic

An element is **diegetic** when it exists inside the game world, so the
characters could see or hear it: the crackling of a campfire, a radio in a
room, the hero's footsteps. It is **non-diegetic** when it exists only for the
player: the background music, a narrator's voice, the score counter.

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 2.1 — Diegetic and non-diegetic"}
A media element is **diegetic** if it belongs to the game world and the
characters could notice it. It is **non-diegetic** if only the player can
notice it.
:::

Interfaces can be described in more detail (@fig-diegesis). Some elements are
*placed* in the game world but are not part of the story, such as a name
floating above a character or the "+10" above a coin: they are called
**spatial**. Others are part of the story but not placed in the world, such as
red marks on the screen when the hero is hurt: they are called **meta**.

![Four kinds of interface elements (after Fagerholt and Lorentzon, 2009).](images/diegesis.png){#fig-diegesis width=78%}

Designers choose on purpose. Diegetic elements make the player feel inside the
world (**immersion**), but they can be slower to read. Non-diegetic elements
are clear and quick to read, but they remind the player of the interface.
Horror games often hide the HUD and use diegetic signs instead: the hero
breathes heavily instead of showing a health bar.

::: {.callout-note title="Example 2.3 — The sounds of one scene"}
In *Ember Trail*, the fox walks past a campfire at night.

1. The crackling of the fire, louder when the fox comes closer: **diegetic**.
   The fox could hear it, and it comes from a place in the world.
2. The fox's footsteps: **diegetic**.
3. The flute music: **non-diegetic**. There is no flute in the world.
4. The "ting" of a collected coin: **non-diegetic** feedback, even though the
   coin itself is in the world.
:::

{{< sim file="sims/sound-stage.html" poster="sims/sound-stage.png" title="Sound Stage: inside or outside the world?" kind="game" height="560" >}}

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Sound Stage"}
Open the **Sound Stage** mini-game above (or scan its QR code). Use
headphones if you can.

1. Walk the fox past the campfire. Switch each layer on and off.
2. Write which sounds change when the fox moves, and which stay the same.

*Your result:* two lists (diegetic, non-diegetic) and one sentence: how can you
hear the difference?
:::

## Case study: analysing Ember Trail

*Ember Trail* is a made-up 2D adventure game for phones. A young fox crosses a
forest at night to go home. The art style is soft and round, the colours are
warm against deep blue, and the music is a solo flute with wind sounds. The
interface shows health, coins and a pause button. Short animated scenes tell
the story between chapters. The Game challenge of the interactive lesson
analyses it with the method of this lesson.

## Further reading

Schell, *The Art of Game Design*, 3rd ed., the chapters on aesthetics and on
the interface; Collins, *Game Sound*, MIT Press, 2008, on diegetic and
non-diegetic game sound.

## Exercises

1. Name the five media channels. Give one example of each from a game you
   know.
2. Write a four-row inventory of the title screen of a game you know.
3. Name the five functions of media. Give one element with two functions and
   explain both.
4. Rewrite "The game has sound effects" as a sentence that explains the role
   of one sound for the player.
5. Diegetic or non-diegetic? (a) a radio in a car that the player drives;
   (b) the menu music; (c) a narrator; (d) a dog that barks behind a wall.
6. Give one advantage and one disadvantage of replacing the HUD with diegetic
   elements.
7. *Ember Trail*: name two media elements that tell the story, and say how.

## Answers to the exercises

::: {.answers}
1. Visual (art style), audio (music), text and story (dialogue), cinematic (cut-scene), interface (HUD).
2. For example: logo (visual), theme music (audio), "Tap to start" (interface), moving background (visual).
3. Feedback, guidance, mood, story, identity. A victory tune: feedback (the level is complete) and identity (players know the tune).
4. For example: "A sharp metal sound confirms every block, so the player knows at once that the attack failed."
5. (a) diegetic; (b) non-diegetic; (c) non-diegetic; (d) diegetic.
6. Advantage: the player feels more inside the world. Disadvantage: the information is slower or harder to read.
7. For example: the speech bubble "The bridge is out!" (text) and the animated scenes between chapters (cinematic) tell where the fox must go and why.
:::
